title: AAST terminology gap supplement — instrumentation foundations
sourceRole: Learner-ready Sleep Pathways Guild definitions for high-value sleep-technology terms identified from the AAST terminology inventory and cross-checked against current AASM Scoring Manual Version 3 usage where applicable.
apaReference: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
aasmReference: Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
copyrightBoundary: Term names and abbreviations are factual inventory data. Definitions and memory clues in this file are original Sleep Pathways Guild summaries and do not reproduce published AAST or AASM definitions.
reviewFocus: Signals, filters, digital acquisition, electrode derivations, sensor concepts, and electrode-placement landmarks.

items.definition: An amplifier used for changing biopotential signals whose frequency response is shaped by low- and high-frequency filtering so selected portions of the signal can be displayed and recorded.
items.memoryClue: AC amplifier = changing signals plus filter limits.

items.definition: The part of a digital recording system that samples a continuous analog signal at set time intervals and assigns numeric amplitude values so the waveform can be stored and displayed digitally.
items.memoryClue: ADC turns continuous voltage into sampled numbers.

items.definition: An amplifier that compares the voltages present at two inputs and amplifies the difference between them; a PSG channel therefore represents the voltage difference between its two electrode inputs.
items.memoryClue: Two inputs in, voltage difference out.

items.definition: The upper-frequency cutoff control that progressively reduces activity above the selected cutoff. Functionally, it behaves as a low-pass filter.
items.memoryClue: HFF cuts the highs.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The lower-frequency cutoff control that reduces slow activity below the selected cutoff. Functionally, it behaves as a high-pass filter.
items.memoryClue: LFF cuts the lows.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A narrow-band filter used to suppress power-line interference around the local mains frequency, commonly 60 Hz in the United States. It can hide electrical contamination, so it should not replace troubleshooting the signal source.
items.memoryClue: Notch = narrow slice removed around line noise.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The sampling principle that a signal frequency requires a sampling rate of at least twice that frequency to be represented without aliasing.
items.memoryClue: Sample at least 2× the highest frequency of interest.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: Opposition to alternating current at an electrode or circuit interface. Excessive or poorly balanced electrode impedance can increase noise and reduce recording quality.
items.memoryClue: Impedance is opposition to AC; lower and balanced is cleaner.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The display scale relating an input voltage to the height of the recorded waveform. Changing sensitivity changes how large the trace appears, not the biological voltage itself.
items.memoryClue: Sensitivity changes the display scale, not the patient signal.

items.definition: The positive-or-negative direction assigned to a voltage difference. In standard PSG display convention, a relatively negative voltage at the first input produces an upward deflection.
items.memoryClue: PSG convention: negative at input 1 goes up.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A digital acquisition method in which electrode signals are initially recorded against a common reference and later recombined mathematically to display the desired derivations.
items.memoryClue: Record to one common reference, then re-derive digitally.

items.definition: A channel formed by comparing an active electrode with a reference electrode at another site, such as C3-M2.
items.memoryClue: Active site compared with a reference site.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: An electrode used as the comparison input in a derivation. In recommended AASM EEG derivations, the mastoid electrodes M1 and M2 commonly serve as references.
items.memoryClue: Reference electrode = the comparison point.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The planned selection and display order of recording channels or derivations, together with the settings used to view the physiologic signals.
items.memoryClue: Montage = which channels are displayed and how they are arranged.

items.definition: One millionth of a volt, written 10^-6 V. Microvolts are commonly used to describe the amplitude of EEG, EOG, and EMG signals.
items.memoryClue: Micro = one millionth.

items.definition: Electrical potential difference between two points. A PSG channel displays how the voltage difference between its inputs changes over time.
items.memoryClue: Voltage is a difference in electrical potential.

items.definition: The overall shape and appearance of a waveform produced by its frequency components, amplitude, and phase relationships. Morphology helps distinguish expected physiologic patterns from artifact.
items.memoryClue: Morphology means the waveform's shape.

items.definition: The SI unit used to express electrical resistance and impedance.
items.memoryClue: Ohm measures opposition to current.

items.definition: The electrical relationship V = I × R, linking voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit.
items.memoryClue: V = I × R.

items.definition: A temperature-sensitive resistive sensor that detects the temperature change between inspired and expired air and can therefore serve as a thermal airflow signal.
items.memoryClue: Thermistor senses airflow through temperature-dependent resistance.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A thermal airflow sensor made from dissimilar metals that produces an electrical signal related to temperature differences between inspired and expired air.
items.memoryClue: Thermocouple = two metals sensing temperature change.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A sensor that generates an electrical signal when its material is mechanically deformed. In PSG, piezoelectric sensing can be used to detect vibration or movement such as snoring.
items.memoryClue: Mechanical stress becomes an electrical signal.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A flexible polyvinylidene fluoride sensor that converts physical changes into an electrical signal and may be configured to monitor airflow or thoracoabdominal effort depending on the sensor design.
items.memoryClue: PVDF is a flexible sensor material used for airflow or effort signals.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The midline depression at the bridge of the nose where the frontal and nasal bones meet; it is one of the landmarks used for standardized head measurements in electrode placement.
items.memoryClue: Nasion = front midline landmark at the bridge of the nose.

items.definition: The palpable midline bony prominence at the back of the skull used as a landmark for standardized electrode-placement measurements.
items.memoryClue: Inion = back-of-head midline landmark.

items.definition: The outer corner of the eye, used as an anatomic landmark when positioning EOG electrodes.
items.memoryClue: Outer canthus anchors EOG placement.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A landmark immediately in front of the ear used for left-to-right head measurements in standardized electrode-placement systems.
items.memoryClue: Preauricular = just in front of the ear.

items.definition: A muscle located between adjacent ribs that contributes to breathing. In selected physiologic recordings, intercostal EMG can reflect respiratory muscle activity.
items.memoryClue: Intercostal = between the ribs.

items.definition: The volume of air moved during a typical breath. In PSG, thoracoabdominal effort signals may estimate relative changes in tidal volume but do not ordinarily provide a direct absolute volume measurement.
items.memoryClue: Tidal volume = air moved in one normal breath.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
